messages.content: "In a game of basketball, a player has a 60% chance of making a successful shot. In a particular match, the player attempts 10 shots. What is the probability that the player makes exactly 6 successful shots? Now, consider a different scenario where the player's success rate drops to 50% but the number of attempts remains the same. What is the probability of making exactly 6 successful shots in this scenario? Finally, consider a third scenario where the player's success rate remains at 50% but the number of attempts increases to 15. What is the probability of making exactly 6 successful shots in this third scenario?"

function.name: calc_binomial_prob
function.description: Calculates the probability of an outcome based on the binomial distribution Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

num_success.description: Number of times the event of interest has occurred.

prob_success.description: Probability of the event of interest on any single experiment. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Binomial‑distribution framework**

For \(n\) independent trials each having success probability \(p\),  
the probability of obtaining exactly \(k\) successes is  

\[
P(X=k)= \binom{\,n\,}{\,k\,}\;p^{\,k}(1-p)^{\,n-k}
      = {n!\over k!(n-k)!}\;p^{\,k}(1-p)^{\,n-k}.
\]

Below we apply it to the three scenarios you described.



| # | Parameters | Formula | Numerical result |
|---|------------|---------|------------------|
| **1** | \(n=10,\;p=0.60,\;k=6\) | \(\displaystyle \binom{10}{6}(0.6)^6(0.4)^4\) | \(\boxed{\approx 0.2512}\) |
| **2** | \(n=10,\;p=0.50,\;k=6\) | \(\displaystyle \binom{10}{6}(0.5)^6(0.5)^4\) | \(\boxed{\approx 0.2051}\) |
| **3** | \(n=15,\;p=0.50,\;k=6\) | \(\displaystyle \binom{15}{6}(0.5)^6(0.5)^9\) | \(\boxed{\approx 0.1527}\) |

---

### How the numbers were obtained

#### Scenario 1 – 10 shots, 60 % accuracy

\[
\begin{aligned}
\binom{10}{6}&=\frac{10!}{6!\,4!}=210\\[4pt]
P_1 &=210\times(0.6)^6\times(0.4)^4   \\[4pt]
    &\approx 210\times0.046656\times0.0256\\[4pt]
    &\approx 210\times0.001195\\[4pt]
    &\approx 0.2512 .
\end{aligned}
\]

> **Interpretation:** About one out of four players who shoot ten baskets with a 60 % free‑throw percentage will hit exactly six of them.


#### Scenario 2 – 10 shots, 50 % accuracy

Because \(p=q=0.5\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_2&=210\times(0.5)^6\times(0.5)^4\\
   &=210\times(0.5)^{10}\\
   &=210\times\frac{1}{1024}\\
   &\approx 0.2051 .
\end{aligned}
\]

> **Interpretation:** With a flat 50 % shooting streak, the odds drop slightly compared to the higher skill level in Scenario 1.


#### Scenario 3 – 15 shots, 50 % accuracy

Here the combinatorial factor grows because there are many more ways to pick which 6 of the 15 shots succeed.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\binom{15}{6}&=\frac{15!}{6!\,9!}=5005\\[4pt]
P_3&=5005\times(0.5)^6\times(0.5)^9\\
   &=5005\times(0.5)^{15}\\
   &=5005\times\frac{1}{32768}\\
   &\approx 0.1527 .
\end{aligned}
\]

> **Interpretation:** Even though the per‑shot success rate stays at 50 %, increasing the total number of attempts from 10 to 15 reduces the likelihood of hitting exactly six baskets—because “exactly six” becomes relatively rarer when you have more chances overall.

---

These figures illustrate how both the individual success probability (\(p\)) and the total number of trials (\(n\)) shape the distribution of outcomes under a binomial process.
